en: Shi Dunlun’s *Collected Explanations of the Treatise*, Volume Twenty-nine.
From here below is the second section: Explaining Right Effort (*samyakprahāṇa*). The text is divided into two parts: first, concluding what was previously explained; second, [the main exposition].
From this point forward, the section beginning with "immediately thereafter" clarifies the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Regarding the first of these, it says: "one eliminates coarse [afflictions] and dispels coarse inversions by thoroughly understanding wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Master Tai’s commentary explains this as follows:
The Sanskrit term has multiple meanings;
for instance, it can mean "moment by moment," while here it is translated as "coarse."
The meaning is also like this.
Furthermore, it is explained that because the four inversions are not singular, they must be stated repeatedly.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that because the inversions are coarse, deep, and heavy, they are called "coarse-coarse. Moreover,
because the preceding thought-moment has already discerned whether the hindrances and fetters exist or not, one thereby thoroughly understands what is unwholesome.
Because one thoroughly understands the presence and absence of the seven factors of enlightenment, one fully realizes wholesome dharmas.
In the second section of the text,
this is first explained in detail.
Second, the brief explanation of the meaning.
Within this, there are again two parts.
First, the individual explanation of the four kinds of right exertion (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Second, the general explanation of the name.
Within this, first the terms are listed and subsequently explained.
From "uninterrupted" up to "gathering the mind and maintaining the mind," [the terms are as follows].
If one follows the full enumeration of names provided in the preceding fascicle:

first, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, arouses diligence, and applies oneself with vigor to restrain the mind and maintain it—this is right abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Second, for the sake of preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising, one generates desire, exerts effort, and so forth.
Third, for the sake of causing unarisen wholesome states to arise, one generates desire, exerts effort, and so forth.

Fourth, regarding wholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, and so forth, in order to maintain them, prevent their loss, bring them to fulfillment through cultivation, cause them to be practiced repeatedly, and cause them to increase and expand.
In this present text, the non-arising of unwholesome and unvirtuous states is first clarified, followed by the analysis of those already arisen.
Within the subsequent explanation,
the nature of the wholesome and unwholesome, as well as the arisen and the unarisen, is initially elucidated.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of abandoning evil and cultivating good through generating desire, exertion, and so forth:
within the former [section], one first explains the arising and non-arising of unwholesome dharmas;
subsequently, one explains the arising and non-arising of wholesome dharmas.
And those that can give rise to all their respective afflictions— namely,
the entirety of those arising from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) and a portion of those arising from cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which are capable of inciting unwholesome conduct—
[are abandoned] within the state where wholesome dharmas have arisen or have not yet arisen.
Regarding the statement, "What are called all wholesome dharmas? They are those which serve as their antidotes," etc.:
the first phrase refers to the general antidote, while the following two phrases refer to the specific antidotes.
Regarding the phrase "that [person]," Master Ki provided two interpretations.
The first states:
This refers specifically to that [state],
namely those fetters and bonds.
Another explanation says:
The preceding section explained unwholesome dharmas;
the present section concerns their respective antidotes.
The final two lines specifically identify the factors that serve as these antidotes.
The first phrase constitutes the general summary.
Next is the explanation of "generating desire, exerting effort," and so forth;
this section is divided into two parts.
In the first stage of understanding, one generates desire, exerts oneself, and arouses diligent effort;
in the subsequent stage of understanding, one restrains the mind and sustains the mind.
Within the former [stage], there are further two [aspects].
The first interpretation concerns the severing of evil and the arising of desire, etc.;
the latter interpretation concerns the arising of good and the arising of desire, etc.
Within the former, there are two parts.
The first explanation gives rise to a desire [to know].
As for the phrase "all and all," it refers to all evil karma and all afflictions; thus it is stated twice.
Furthermore,
it is explained as all births and all formations (*saṃskāra*).
Next, the explanation of exerting oneself and arousing diligent effort consists of four sections.
The first section clarifies that regarding the objects of past and future conditions— those unwholesome and evil dharmas that are not presently perceived—
one desires that those which have not yet arisen do not arise,
and one desires that those which have already arisen be permanently severed.
This is called exertion:
regarding those evil and unwholesome states that are presently perceived as objects,
one ensures that those which have not yet arisen do not arise.
Having arisen, one exerts diligent effort for their permanent abandonment.

The third section clarifies that regarding the first two right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), when practicing with respect to objects in the past or future in this manner, one does not allow afflictions to arise in relation to them; even if they should momentarily arise, one is able to swiftly eliminate them—this is called "exertion" (*vyāyāma*).

If, while practicing in the present, one does not allow afflictions to arise in relation to those objects, and if they do arise, they are quickly extinguished—this is called "exerting diligent effort.

The fourth section clarifies that regarding evil and unwholesome dharmas, whether past or future, by the power of conceptualization rather than the power of the object: to prevent those not yet arisen from arising, and to cause those already arisen to be abandoned, is called "striving."

If, regarding the present, one exerts diligent effort so that what has not yet arisen does not arise through the power of conceptualization and the power of objects, and so that what has already arisen is permanently severed—
Master Ji explains this as follows:
"Arising solely through the power of conceptualization and not through the power of objects" refers to those who, while dwelling [in the present], contemplate the past and so forth;
that is, they do not engage with objects, as there is no engagement with non-existent objects.
However, because it takes the past and future as its object, it is called "abiding.
Furthermore, regarding the power of discrimination and the power of the objective sphere:
that which proceeds toward an objective sphere is called "proceeding" (*saṃskāra*).
Since there is necessarily conceptualization when the power of the objects of unwholesome dharmas arises,
this specific phrase [“unwholesome dharmas arise from conceptualization”] is omitted. That “conceptualization itself arises as unwholesome and so forth” is the first specific phrase.
Taking the past and future as objects, a second "concurrent" category arises;
its arising with respect to present objects is explained as the inverse of the first [category],
and its application of exertion and diligence is the same.
The subsequent explanation concerns the arising of wholesome states, the arising of desire, and so forth.
Within this, there are further two parts;
first is the explanation of the arising of desire.
Next, the exegesis on "exerting oneself with diligence" follows,
explaining the text in its entirety.
Within this exegesis on exerting oneself with diligence:
Third, the explanation.

From here on is the second section, the interpretation of "exerting the mind" and "sustaining the mind," which explains these generally in terms of abandoning two evils and giving rise to two virtues.
If [the mind] sinks, one should exert it;
if it becomes agitated, one should steady it.
Having thus separately explained the four kinds of right abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*), [the text continues].
The following explains the general name,
which has two designations:
the first is "Right Exertion" (samyakprahāṇa).
Because they overcome the afflictions,
they are called "right abandonments" (samyakprahāṇa),
for they eliminate the afflictions.
Regarding the phrase "the restraint of restraint and the abandonment of abandonment," Jing says:
"The curbing of evil is called restraint (*saṃvara*)."
Initially, one cultivates impure diligence to restrain those already arisen unwholesome states so that they do not lead to future consequences;
this is called "abandonment through restraint.
Subsequently, one cultivates pure diligence.
The severance of the seeds perfumed by arisen unwholesome states is also called "restraint through severance.
As for those unwholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, they possess the potential to arise.
In order to sever the manifestation of what is yet to arise, one severs its seeds;
thus it is said to be "for the purpose of severing. Therefore, it is called "severing-severance" (*prahāṇa-prahāṇa*).
Master Ji said:
"Regarding 'the restraint that cuts off [evil]':
restraint is defined as the prevention of transgressions."
It is for the purpose of preventing arisen unwholesome states from increasing and not allowing them to further grow.
To explain individually:
morality is well-purified by means of ten causes and conditions.
This refers to the ten factors conducive to training (*daśa śaikṣadharmāḥ*) found in the preceding twenty-eighth fascicle:
first, avoiding women;
second, avoiding attachment.
Third, freedom from indolence;
fourth, freedom from the view of self;
fifth, freedom from the flavor of solid food.
Sixth, freedom from attachment to discursive speech;
seventh, freedom from the eleven faults;
eighth, freedom from the relish of meditative concentration.
Ninth, freedom from distraction;
tenth, patience.
These are the protectors and abandoners.
This very diligence constitutes the cultivation of heedfulness (*apramāda*),
because it prevents the loss of already arisen wholesome states.
Below this, the second section briefly explains the meaning.
This means that, in order to demonstrate the matters of abandoning and adopting regarding black and white [phenomena], and so forth up to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*),
the preceding [text] is abbreviated for the sake of clarity;
it shows the abandonment of the two black matters.
One takes up two white matters (*śukla-vastu*).
The arising of desire is called the fulfillment of the intention (*āśaya-paripūri*).
Through self-exertion, the arousal of diligent energy (*vīrya*), and the uplifting and sustaining of the mind, it is called the fulfillment of the application (*prayoga-paripūri*).
For the practitioner of yoga, these are the only tasks that ought to be performed, even unto the point of forming a longing desire.
To restate the preceding text more concisely:
one generates a longing desire for the sake of abandoning the three unwholesome actions and cultivating the three wholesome ones.
Regarding the cultivation of the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) in order to sever the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*):

this briefly refers to the preceding passage on maintaining the mind. Because one cultivates the three wholesome states to sever the three unwholesome ones, when the mind sinks, one should immediately apprehend a sign of purity to rouse and uplift the mind.
If, because of exertion, the mind becomes overly agitated, one should stabilize the mind;
this is the application of restraint.
If the mind does not become restless, one should maintain equanimity toward the continuity of the mind, which is able to sever all fetters.

Regarding the statement, "In order to sever the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one should further cultivate the wholesome dharmas that serve as their antidotes":
this briefly refers to the aforementioned cultivation for the purpose of severing the two types of evil—the manifest envelopments and the latent tendencies associated with those envelopments.
Furthermore, one should properly cultivate both the unarisen and the arisen [wholesome states].
Third, the explanation of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*):
therein, first, the characteristics of the four bases of psychic power are explained in detail.
Second, the analysis of the meaning of the *ṛddhipāda* through questions and answers.
Within this, first the names are listed and assigned;
subsequently, they are explained in detail.
Master Ji said:
"The essence of the four bases of psychic power is meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
they are called 'desire' and so forth because these names are derived from their causes."
Furthermore, concentration serves as the basis for the supernormal powers;
therefore, it is called the "basis of supernormal power. Moreover, concentration is itself termed "supernormal" (*ṛddhi*).
These four are the bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) of the mind;
from these bases of spiritual power, the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*) arises.
Master Zhan said:
Furthermore, this may also refer to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Within the second section of the detailed explanation that follows,
the text is divided into three parts.
First, it clarifies that the four contaminated concentrations (*sāsrava-dhyāna*) suppress the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
Second, "By means of these... and so forth below, clarifies that the four uncontaminated concentrations (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) eradicate the seeds (*bīja*).
Third, "In this context, desire" and so forth, clarifies that the eight formative acts of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*) subsume the four yogas.

The beginning and middle state: "If at this time one purely generates the desire for joy, up to the arising of a one-pointed mind," refers to the cultivation of aversion as an antidote toward the intrinsic nature of the obstacles to *samādhi* born of desire, as well as the causes and conditions that obstruct it.
Dedicated to seeking meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
one gives rise to one-pointed mindfulness regarding all wholesome phenomena, up to and including one-pointed mindfulness.

This involves reflecting upon and cultivating the intrinsic nature of the various wholesome qualities and their favorable causes and conditions, while aspiring to practice and abide in one-pointed mindfulness.
This is the skillful means.

That is to say, by means of the causes explained below, one practices in order to attain samādhi; however, while one has merely separated from the manifest fetters (*paryavasthāna*), one has not yet destroyed their seeds.
Next, the abandonment through untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) is explained.

Regarding the statement, "By the power of having cultivated these four samādhis, one becomes distant from the various envelopments (paryavasthāna) up to the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga)," Jing says:
"Although one attains freedom from the various envelopments by means of the four dhyānas that are with outflows (sāsrava),..."
In order to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one further diligently cultivates the various untainted concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*).
Furthermore, separately generating a mind of superior desire and diligence, one contemplates the four causes while cultivating the untainted concentration.
Among these four causes, each one is capable of severing two types of evil and giving rise to two types of goodness,
according to the principle of the application of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

It is said that through two causal conditions, one thoroughly understands the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) by means of reflection on objects that are not directly perceived and by means of equanimity toward objects that are directly perceived.
Among the eight applications for abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), one knows that the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) have been abandoned based solely on the latter two.

This is because, at all times, through the constant cultivation of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) initiated by body and speech, one knows that the mental factors are not manifest and that the mind is already free from the underlying tendencies.

Because one knows how to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the objects of the afflictions throughout the three periods of time without the mind being defiled, it is said: "and because of the relinquishing through the direct perception of the object.
Ji says:
Regarding the phrase "he proceeds thus, even unto the distinctions," this is cited to clarify the basis for the eight formative forces of abandonment (*aṣṭau prahāṇasaṃskārāḥ*).
These eight formative forces were formerly known as the "eight joys" and the "eight requisites."
To clarify the intended meaning, two gates are opened:
first, for the purpose of severing the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
second, for the purpose of perfecting meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In accordance with the explanation below regarding the two kinds of factors that can sever the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
the subsequent text states:
"By means of two causes and conditions, one analytically understands the abandonment of the latent dispositions."

This means that by means of direct observation through reflection (*cintā*) and by means of relinquishing what is not directly perceived (*parokṣa*), one is able to sever the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) through these two conditions.
According to this, it is stated in the explanation of "exertion" (*pragraha*) at the beginning of this fascicle:
If one takes as an object a past or future phenomenon, it is called "taking an unperceived object.
If one takes as an object a present phenomenon, it is called "taking a perceived object.
This principle implies that when one abandons past and future phenomena through reflection, one does so by means of the present.

If that is so, why does the explanation regarding equanimity (*upekṣā*) state: "It refers to the state of equality of the mind that accords with all unwholesome thoughts throughout the three periods of past, future, and present; furthermore, it divides volition (*cetanā*) into one period and equanimity into two periods"?
In fact, as stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-kośa*:

"The antidote refers to volition (*cetanā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), because they can distance one from sinking (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*) once they have arisen; thus, these two dharmas—volition and equanimity—pervade the abandonment of the three time periods. Since they are called the 'abandonment of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*'), [they constitute the antidote]."
The remaining six [factors] should be understood accordingly as the perfection of samādhi.
Furthermore, the subsequent text states:

"If these eight types of exertions (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) now described are fully accomplished for the sake of permanently severing all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are collectively termed 'desire-samādhi' (*chanda-samādhi*)."
Examining this general text, it appears that all eight [mental factors] possess both functions.
Furthermore, they subsume the four yogas because they are capable of severing the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Moreover, volition (*cetanā*) is able to initiate physical and vocal actions, giving rise to wholesome bodily and verbal karma and causing unwholesome bodily and verbal conduct to cease.
Since body and speech are material (*rūpa*), volition (*cetanā*) is designated by way of that materiality; thus, volition is "manifestly perceived" (*pratyakṣa*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*), however, exists only in the mind and is not identical to volition; therefore, it is called "unmanifestly perceived" (*apratyakṣa*).
This does not necessarily accord with the text at the beginning of this fascicle.

These eight kinds of abandoned practices (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) and superior practices (*viśeṣabhāvanā*) constitute the yoga for the practitioner who seeks to eliminate the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Jing says:
"Yoga is also termed 'skillful means' (*upāya*)."
Alternatively, they are called "conformity" (*yoga*) and so forth.
Below, the latter eight will subsume the former four.

The eight abandonments are precisely the twenty-eight yogas from the fourth [chapter] of the previous volume; these are the abilities to abandon the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely: desire, diligence, faith, and skillful means.
Although the *Abhidharma* contains four types of inclusion (*saṃgraha*), they are entirely different [from this system] and cannot be reconciled.
Furthermore, the sequence herein differs from that of the four yogas found within the twenty-eight [sections].
In this context, the sequence of the eight abandonments arises one after another as described in the text.
As stated in the previous fascicle, among the four yogas, faith is the first; the *Abhidharma* is likewise the same.
Therefore, that treatise states that faith is the cause of desire (*chanda*).
The commentary states:
When establishing desire and diligence, one is not separated from faith;
therefore, faith should be placed at the beginning.
Because desire and the other [mental factors] arise only when faith and the like are present,
and because they are not separated from faith, faith is mentioned last.
This is because the text of the Abhidharma itself reconciles the sequence of arising as taught in the four *yogas*.
Therefore, faith is primary.
Question: For what reason and by what causal conditions is the meaning of the "bases of psychic power" (ṛddhipāda) explained in the second question and answer below?
Why is it called a "base of psychic power" because one is able to reach [the goal] through them?
Jingyun: This teaching states that the name for tainted concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) is "divine" (*divya*),
while desire and so forth are called "bases" (*pāda*).
Thus, the supramundane concentration is distinguished below as the "divine" (ṛddhi);
the separately arising superior desire, exertion, mind, and observation, along with the eight formative forces of abandonment (prahāṇasaṃskāra), are called the "feet.
Tai says:
Concentration can give rise to all supreme dharmas that are meritorious;
it is called "divine" (*ṛddhi*) because it is unfathomable.
Because it can reach these unfathomable merits, it is called a "foot" (*pāda*).
Master Ji said:
"Because they are able to reach these [states], they are called 'possessors of the bases of supernormal power' (ṛddhipāda).
Thus, being able to go and return, and so forth, is what is meant by the fruit of the realm of the bases of supernormal power."
Because desire and so forth serve as the causes for attaining this meditative power (*ṛddhi*),
it is called a "basis of power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
Fourth is the explanation of the faculty and power of resolve (*adhimokṣendriya-bala*).
Within this, there are four parts:
first, explaining the characteristics of the five faculties;
second, explaining the characteristics of the five powers.
Third, a general analysis of the remaining characteristics of equality based on the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*).
Fourth, a general analysis of the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*) based on the faculties and powers.

Regarding the first [of these], it refers to the yoga of training in mind (*citta-śikṣā*) and training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), which follows the sequential cultivation of the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*) through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
By practicing this yoga through diligent cultivation, one develops deep pure faith in the disciples of the Buddha.
This faith has the power to give rise to supramundane dharmas and can initiate subsequent stages, serving as the superior condition for the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Within this context, faith has two types of predominance:
first, it acts as the predominance for the arising of supramundane dharmas;
second, it acts as the predominance for the successive arising of subsequent dharmas.
Therefore, they are called faculties (*indriya*).
The first four possess both meanings;
thus, diligence and the others also function as faculties prior [to their respective stages].
That wisdom has but a single meaning;
it serves as the predominant condition solely for the arising of supramundane dharmas,
and is incapable of generating subsequent meanings through successive progression.
Regarding the explanation of the five powers (*pañca-balāni*):
if one further understands that there is a distinction between what was realized previously and what is realized later,
this refers to understanding that the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), which is the initial cause, subsequently gives rise to supramundane dharmas (*lokottara-dharma*).

Next, after having mastered the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), one subsequently realizes supramundane dharmas; this continues up to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), which realizes only supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, it is said that one understands the distinction between what was realized previously and what is realized later.
In general, regarding the discernment of the remaining characteristics within the text concerning the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), there are five phrases.

One should observe that from "the faculty of faith" and "the power of faith" up to "for what reason," the power of faith is with-outflow (*sāsrava*) and exists prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
How does one obtain the faith among the four kinds of verified clarity (*pratisaṃvid*) within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*)?
Therefore, it is asked: "For what reason?
The following explains that through the power of faith, those verified clarities of the path of vision arise.
Because they belong to the same causal continuum, it is said that they "are identical.
This does not mean they are identical in essence or identical in characteristic.
One should contemplate herein the faculty and power of diligence, and so forth.
Among these four roots of goodness, the faculty and power of diligence are precisely the diligence found within the first three skillful means, namely, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
As for the question, "Which right effort is this?"—it refers to the right effort of skillful means (*upāyasamyakprahāṇa*).
Regarding the correct abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), they further rely on the four correct abandonments and the power of diligence within the three preceding applications (*prayoga*).

These draw forth the diligence of the factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) that arises upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), thereby abandoning the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya-kleśa*).
Regarding the statement, "The meaning here is that it refers to the ultimate abandonment of evil and unwholesome states":
the meaning here is that,

through the power of the faculty of diligence, one brings about the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), whereby the factor of enlightenment of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) among the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*) effects the final abandonment of evil.
Therefore, cause and effect are mutually identical in their anteriority and posteriority.
One should observe that within this context, the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) and the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*) extend to all perversions.

The faculty of mindfulness and the power of mindfulness are precisely the right mindfulness found within the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and within the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*).
This means that the four foundations of mindfulness can sever all inversions regarding the truth of suffering and so forth.
The above explains the essence of the four foundations of mindfulness;
they consist of mindfulness and wisdom.
Therefore, the faculty of mindfulness and the power of mindfulness now constitute the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
One should observe that within this context, through the faculty of concentration and the power of concentration, one may even realize the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
Jing says:

The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) and the power of concentration (*samādhibala*) are attained by both those who practice through the sequential method (*anupūrvika*) and those who practice by leaping over (*vyutkrāntaka*).
For those who practice sequentially, the faculty and power of concentration belong to the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
For those who practice by leaping over, they pertain to all four dhyānas; therefore, it is said that they consist of the right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) found within the four dhyānas.
If a transcender relies on the power of the four fundamental dhyānas and, by the power of those fundamental dhyānas, enters the path of seeing and directly realizes the fruit of non-returner,
it is therefore said that the various dhyānas serve as the means for realizing the fruit of non-returner.

To speak briefly, it is not mentioned that by relying on the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*), the faculty of concentration, and the power of concentration as skillful means, one enters the path of seeing and realizes the fruits of stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and so forth.
Jì (基) says:
"In this context, the first two fruits are attained only in the future; proceeding sequentially from there, upon reaching the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), one attains the four dhyānas."
Because they manifest supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), this [text] speaks specifically of these [fruits] and does not mention the fourth fruit.
This is because it is not part of the sequential order, and furthermore, it is implied by the others.
Furthermore, because they are mentioned only briefly,
it is said that within the four dhyānas one generates the supernormal powers and the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda),
but not in other meditative concentrations.
One should observe that the faculty of wisdom and the power of wisdom herein lead to the attainment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya;
for the faculty of wisdom and the power of wisdom prior to the path of seeing are themselves the knowledge within the path of seeing.
It is by means of the faculty of wisdom and the power of wisdom from the preceding stage that noble knowledge is induced, thereby attaining the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Therefore, cause and effect are mutually identical in their anteriority and posteriority.
Regarding the fourth section, which generally distinguishes the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) by means of the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*),
Jing says:
If one considers them according to their predominance, these five faculties are precisely the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan).
Since they take their initial arising as the basis,
the five faculties are established within the stages of Heat and Summits.
The patience (*kṣānti*) and the first proximate birth (*anantarya-janman*) that gives rise to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are difficult to subdue; however,
in this present text, both the strong and the weak are discussed together.
Whether as faculties (*indriya*) or powers (*bala*), they pertain to all four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
That which has the sense of being able to produce [wholesome states] is called a faculty;
that which has the sense of being unbending and difficult to subdue is called a power.
These faculties and powers are the very essence of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*).

Regarding the statement that "it is precisely by means of the repeated cultivation of these faculties and powers that the four roots of goodness are initiated," this refers to the stage of the completion of practice (*pratipatti-siddhi-avasthā*). Furthermore, Master Ki says:
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) herein, they are as described in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*:
the faculties are present during the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), while the powers are present in the two subsequent stages.
As for the statement "up to this point," it means that by means of these faculties and powers, the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are generated.
These faculties and powers are specific [factors] of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and are general [factors].
Because the specific gives rise to the general, they are called "arising" (*utpāda*).
This is because they arise simultaneously rather than at different times; arising sequentially, one after another, is termed "initiation" (*samutthāna*).
Some say that one attains the untainted (anāsrava) state prior to the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
As stated in the subsequent section of the treatise: "By the power of the faculties (indriya), the supramundane untainted noble dharmas (lokottara-anāsrava-āryadharma) arise immediately thereafter."
Therefore, one should know that what precedes this is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and cannot be called without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Fifth is the awakening factor of investigation (*dharma-vicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). What, then, is this?
Jingyun: The five powers (pañcabala) have already been analyzed within the "Dharma of the Categories of the Path" (mārgāṅga).
This statement is made because one further clarifies what dharma follows these five powers.
Now, one should know that the separate mention of "untainted noble dharmas" (*anāsrava-āryadharma*) in the preceding chapter is likewise so.
Therefore, it asks: "Furthermore, what is this?"
Regarding the statement, "The seven factors of enlightenment... are thus called 'factors of enlightenment'":
this text explains that the wisdom of the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) is both awakening itself and a factor of enlightenment.
The remaining six are factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) but are not enlightenment itself;
their mutual inclusion according to the three aspects is as stated in the text.
The lower section, consisting of ninety-eight [items], illustrates this by means of the metaphor of the seven treasures of a wheel-turning monarch;
it should be examined.
Sixth, the explanation of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Regarding the initial statement, "Having seen the tracks of the Noble Truths, [craving] is forever severed and extinguished," etc.,
this serves as a transition from the preceding to the subsequent section in order to clarify the eightfold path.
Within the main exposition, the text is divided into five parts.
First, the inclusion within the three aggregates;
second, the explanation of the meaning of the factors of the path;
third, the analysis of the characteristics of the factors of the path.
Fourth, the general establishment of two types;
fifth, the position of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Regarding those subsumed under the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), namely right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*):
Because mindfulness conforms to concentration (*samādhi*), it is now categorized as the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*).

Within the section on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), mindfulness pertains to both categories; why, then, is the mindfulness of this factor of the path (*mārgāṅga*) specifically subsumed under concentration?
This is because the former was distinguished according to the gates of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Later, they are distinguished by way of the three aggregates;
thus, their meanings differ.
Within the analysis of their characteristics:
Regarding the statement, "One should know that herein, when the time for the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) has arrived, they are collectively termed Right View," the Tripiṭaka Master says:
this refers to the true discernment of dharmas (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) attained during the seven factors of enlightenment at the stage of the Path of True Seeing (darśanamārga).

Now, subsequent to the path of seeing (darśanamārga), one establishes meditative cultivation through subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna), awakening in a manner that accords with the true realization of the path of seeing;
therefore, these two types of awakening are collectively termed "perfect awakening" (samyagbodhi).
Now, within the cultivation of the path, right view is also twofold:
first, the right view of non-conceptual wisdom;
second, the right view of subsequently attained wisdom.
When that true seeing is established and seen in accordance with reality,
it is termed right view. As for right thought, if it is associated with non-conceptual wisdom,
then that non-conceptual wisdom and the thought itself, being free from wrong thought, are termed right thought.
If one engages in correct reflection with subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) or with a distracted mind,
this is called "correct reflection" by virtue of the conceptualizing wisdom (*vikalpa-prajñā*) involved in that reflection.
If the mind enters into all objects of discursive thought (*vitarka*), it reaches the state of all such volitions (*cetanā*).
This refers to the essence of correct reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) mentioned previously;
specifically, it is based on the essence of correct reflection within the mind of subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), and thus it is said that one "investigates such characteristics.
Furthermore, when the mind enters into all that is expressed in discourse, this is called "right speech" (*samyag-vāc*).
Due to the power of right view arising from the two preceding types of awakening, all subsequent wholesome states of mind that produce various forms of speech are termed "right speech.
This passage explains that speech produced by a distracted mind when free from hatred and delusion is called right speech.
The following clarifies right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
Jing says:

"This clarifies that various bodily actions arising within a distracted mind that is free from hatred and delusion, and which are characterized by right awareness (*samyak-saṃprajanya*), are called right action."
Basibandhu said:
"If one seeks clothing, food, drink, and so forth, up to the requisites for the body, at the time of seeking, this is precisely what is sought at the time of seeking."
Whether going or returning, down to the point of "or while staying"— this refers to what is done while staying.
It is contrary to the twenty-two [cases] and has not been cross-referenced.
Now, examining the twenty-second fascicle:

it clarifies that the expedient means of improperly seeking clothing, food, drink, and so forth, while manifesting as if one already possesses virtuous qualities, are called "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*).
The opposite of this is precisely "right livelihood" (*samyagājīva*).
Now, this text states that when seeking [livelihood] in accordance with the Dharma while dwelling in right awareness, it is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
The opposite of this is wrong action (*mithyā-karmānta*).

Below, it clarifies that when seeking [livelihood] in accordance with the Dharma, being free from the factors that give rise to wrong livelihood (*mithyā-ājīva*) is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
That is to say, the two types of action—bodily and vocal—that arise from non-attachment and consist in the complete abandonment of the factors of wrong livelihood are called right livelihood;
the opposite of this constitutes wrong livelihood.
This explains "dwelling with clear comprehension."
As stated in the twenty-fourth fascicle,
there is therefore no contradiction.
If one distances oneself from [unwholesome conduct] and adopts right speech, action, and livelihood that have already been previously attained;
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), right speech, action, and livelihood are comprised within the category of "separation" (*viveka*).
These have already been previously acquired when one realizes the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Question: Why is this called the "precept beloved by the Noble Ones" (*āryakānta-śīla*) and so forth?
This explains why right speech, action, and livelihood are termed "precepts beloved by the noble ones.
Regarding the phrase "the restraint of non-action," this untainted precept associated with the Path is called the "restraint of non-action."

Precisely by the power of such virtue cherished by the noble ones, all outflow-tainted verbal actions, bodily actions, and livelihood activities present at the time of cultivating the path are designated as right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Regarding the phrase "by the predominant power of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including right concentration," Zhiyi states:
"The meaning here is that,
with the four foundations of mindfulness as the cause, nine kinds of mindfulness arise simultaneously with the concentrated mind."
The ninefold mindfulness is identical to the mindfulness of abiding;
it coexists with the ninefold concentration,
for all nine take concentration as their auxiliary companion.
There are also nine kinds.
Among these two types established through analysis— the primary factor as that which grasps and the accompanying factors as that which is grasped—
[the former] is the grasper and [the latter] is the grasped.
What is called "non-action" refers to right speech, action, and livelihood.

Because one is able, through the faculty of volition, to distance oneself from wrong speech, action, and livelihood such that there is no further activity, it is termed "non-action"; it possesses no separate substantial entity beyond this.
Regarding the five remaining modes of activity of the dwelling-place (*vihāra*), three are contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and two are tranquility (*śamatha*).
That which possesses both substance and capability is called the "activity of the dwelling-place. This is explained within the section on the "determination of states" (*avasthā-viniścaya*).
It is explained that by relying on the precepts, one cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to sever the fetters and attain the state of an Arhat.
The continuous cultivation of the path over a long period to sever delusions is called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The sudden arising of wisdom that results in the permanent severance [of delusions] is called the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This text serves as proof that the "one-mind path of seeing" (*ekacitta-darśanamārga*) is the ultimate teaching, or what is termed the "path of seeing.
For this reason, it is established only at this point:

because during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is a time of emerging from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*), when right speech and so forth arise; this demonstrates that right speech and so forth exist within the state of absorption itself.
Therefore, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are established [as factors of the path].
Since one does not arise from the contemplation of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) to initiate right speech and so forth,
they are not established [therein].

Furthermore, during the long duration of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the continuity [of practice] must necessarily rely upon the precepts (*śīla*) to cultivate calm (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), thereby exhausting the afflictions of cultivation and realizing the latter three fruits.
Therefore, it is only within the path of cultivation that the precepts are formally established.
Because the wisdom that arises abruptly through that Path of Seeing immediately severs the delusions of view, the precepts are not established [as a separate fruit].
This concludes the summary below.
Thirteenth: Explaining the fruit of cultivation.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the clarification of the fruit of cultivation;
second, "Furthermore, within this... and so forth.
Regarding the clarification of the fruits of cultivation, there are further distinctions such as the predominance of afflictions, the balanced type (*sāmya*), and the thin-dust type (*tanu-rajas*).
Within this, the first part consists of the question, followed by the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
The explanation contains two sections.
First, the names of the four fruits are listed and their essential natures are set forth.
Second, the causes and conditions for establishing these fruits are analyzed through questions and answers.
Regarding the first of these, the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer):

Because they have abandoned the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and realized the direct intuition of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), thereby entering the lineage of the noble ones (*āryagotra*),
they are called "Stream-enterers" (*srotāpanna*).
As for the "Once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*), it is as when one attains the second fruit while remaining among humans and is subsequently reborn in the heavenly realms.
Because they attain parinirvāṇa after returning once more to the human realm,
they are called "once-returners" (sakṛdāgāmin).
Having already abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm, they are reborn in the higher realms and do not return [to the desire realm].
Therefore, they are called "Non-returners" (Anāgāmin).
An Arhat is here translated as "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
Because they are fully endowed with wisdom and abandonment and are worthy of offerings,
they are called "Arhats" (Worthy of Offerings).
They are also termed "Slayers of Thieves" or "Those Who Are Not Reborn."
As is usually distinguished:
the noble path is called the śramaṇa, and the abandonment of afflictions is called the fruit.
One who is progressing toward the noble path is called a śramaṇa.
"Śramaṇa" is translated here as "one who exerts effort.
It is so called because through diligent and arduous practice, evil is extinguished and goodness is produced.
The cessation resulting from the abandonment of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), which is attained through analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), is termed the fruit.

In this context, the term "unconditioned fruit" (asaṃskṛta-phala) is a metaphorical designation for the cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) at the point where delusions are abandoned in accordance with suchness.
Furthermore, a subsequently arising path—whether intermediate or superior—is the fruit produced by a previously arisen path.

This refers to the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), whether intermediate or superior, which is the conditioned fruit obtained through the power of the preceding path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga).
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "By the power of the path of uninterrupted transition, one obtains conditioned and unconditioned fruits."
Next, the establishment of the causes and conditions for the fruits is explained.
Four fruits are established in order to counteract four types of afflictions;
the following passage sets forth those four types of afflictions to be countered.

This refers to those who, from the state of having no objective basis (*anupadhiśeṣa*) up to the establishment of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), [overcome] the afflictions of view within the three realms, of which the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the foremost.
This view conceives of a self; it is a one-sided perversion that conceives of existence where there is none.
Because one conceives of a self where no self exists, it is called "non-existent" (*avastuka*).
Therefore, the views and delusions termed "non-existent" are afflictions that lack a real basis;
these non-existent afflictions are capable of dragging one into the evil realms.
Now, the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala) is established based on the severance of these afflictions and the cultivation and arising of their respective counteractive paths;
this is explained according to the *Pañcāśatikā-śāstra*.
There are ten [afflictions] below the stage of suffering (*duḥkha*).
There are eight [afflictions] for each of the three truths;
there are six that are abandoned through cultivation.
According to the Abhidharma, in the desire realm, there are ten afflictions for each of the four [categories], beginning with the "lower" [level].
There are six types of abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), totaling forty-six.
In the five lower categories of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), anger is excluded from each, resulting in forty-one for each.
There are one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions in total across the three realms;
among them, sixteen are abandoned through cultivation,
while the remaining one hundred and twelve are abandoned through insight.
The fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) has been fully attained.
Why, then, did the Blessed One establish the fruit of stream-entry by teaching only the permanent abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*)?
To resolve this objection, it is said: "And the Bhagavān taught," and so forth.
The meaning of the phrasing is clear.
Regarding this "stream-enterer whose continuity extends through many births," it refers specifically to one who has reached the maximum limit of seven births;
such a person is designated as "one whose continuity extends through many births."
If one severs the afflictions that cause the continuity of rebirth up to the point of establishing the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*),
the cultivated afflictions of the desire realm are divided into nine grades.
For the time being, this is discussed on the basis of fourteen births.
If one abandons the first three [fetters], six births remain;
if one abandons the fifth, one will necessarily abandon the sixth within a single lifetime.
Furthermore, by reducing two births, one realizes the second fruit.
The remaining two births are termed "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*);
having attained the fruit among humans, one goes once to the heavens and returns once to the human realm to attain *parinirvāṇa*,
which is termed the fruit of once-returning.
If those two categories of five and six [defilements] were not abandoned, one would still undergo the continuity of rebirth in the realms of gods and humans;

now that these two categories of five and six defilements are abandoned, this constitutes the permanent severance of all defilements pertaining to the continuity of rebirth in the realms of gods and humans.
If one has already eternally severed those defilements capable of causing rebirth and has attained the state of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*),
yet fails to eternally sever the final three grades of defilement, they will return to the desire realm.
Now that it has been permanently severed, it will not arise again;
one will only take birth among the gods of the form and formless realms.
Master Ji further stated: "One will only take birth among the gods."
One type of person, having been in the heavens, receives one more existence among humans; not returning to be born again in the heavens, they are called a Non-returner (Anāgāmin).
Herein, the practice is undertaken based on being among humans.
This is named after its fruit because, at the time of the cause, it is not yet designated as "non-returner.
If one has permanently abandoned the afflictions that induce birth in the realms of form and formlessness, one is established as an Arhat.
The subsequent citations are introduced to provide proof;
however, they only establish the latter three [results].
The citation proving the first fruit has already been explained as before.
Therefore, it is not mentioned here.
Alternatively, one may speak based on what preceded, saying that while a stream-enterer has already severed the three fetters,
they now further proceed to sever the afflictions of cultivation.
The first six categories—greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth—abide in the subsequent three proofs for realizing the fruit of once-returner;
thus it is said that one has "permanently severed the three fetters and attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion.
Furthermore, a stream-enterer first severs the three fetters among the five lower-tier fetters.
The person who has attained the fruit of once-returning further abandons the first six categories of greed and anger;
now, they further abandon the latter three categories of the two fetters of greed and anger.
Because this builds upon the previous [abandonment], it is said that by abandoning the five lower fetters, one establishes the fruit of non-returning.
This person who has attained the fruit of non-returning has already abandoned the afflictions of insight regarding the three realms and the afflictions of cultivation pertaining to the desire realm;
now, they further abandon the eight stages of afflictions of cultivation belonging to the form and formless realms.
Because it follows from what preceded, it is said that by permanently severing all afflictions, the fourth fruit is established.

From here on, the second section clarifies the distinctions among those who have attained the fruits of cultivation, such as those for whom afflictions are predominant or those who possess balanced faculties.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, a distinction between the practices of the seven types of persons;
second, a detailed analysis through questions and answers regarding the differences in the characteristics of those with equal proportions of defilements and those with thin defilements.
The preceding section is divided into seven parts, categorized into three groups:
first, those in whom afflictions predominate;
second, those who are of equal proportions.
Third is the "thin-dust" [type].
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "even up to diligently cultivating the preparatory application (*prayoga*) therein":

for a practitioner in whom greed and so forth are particularly predominant, they should first rely upon those objects of focus for pure conduct (*śubha-nimitta*) to purify their practice; only then will the mind abide in peace.
If one has excessive greed, one should personally contemplate impurity;
if one has excessive anger, one should personally cultivate loving-kindness and compassion;
if one has excessive delusion, one should personally contemplate dependent origination.
Those who are prone to self-conceit observe the six elements;
those who are prone to discursive thought observe the breath.
Therefore, it is said that they each cultivate their respective applications with distinct objects of focus.
As explained extensively above in the treatise:

if a practitioner of the balanced temperament (*sabhāga-carita*) follows their own inclinations and diligently applies themselves to the practice by taking that object as a focal point, such diligent cultivation merely causes the mind to abide, but does not purify the practitioner.
For a practitioner of equal proportions, the afflictions that arise do not increase disproportionately;
thus, they need not specifically contemplate objects such as the impure.
Rather, they should simply abide the mind by contemplating impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and so forth, according to their preference.
It is not like those who, being biased toward one [defilement], separately purify their conduct;
therefore, it is said that they do not purify their conduct.
This is likewise true for those who practice with equal proportions of defilements and those whose conduct is characterized by thin dust.
Yet those various types of conduct differ from one another.

For one whose conduct is dominated by greed and so forth, it takes a long time to attain mental abiding during practice; for one who is balanced, it is not long; and for one with extremely attenuated afflictions, it is very rapid.
Tài said: "The former cultivation of the five *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness) serves as an antidote for increasing delusions;
one must first cultivate self-observation to purify one's own delusions before realizing a concentrated mind."
If one is of the "equal-part" temperament (*samabhāga*), there are no specific afflictions to be remedied;
rather, one should focus on whichever affliction one finds most agreeable,
practicing the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) up to the meditation on the six elements (*ṣaddhātu-bhāvanā*), taking that object as a support and causing the mind to abide therein alone.
Because there are no predominant afflictions to be remedied, it is not a "pure practice" (*śucikarman*).
Baso (基) says:
"Greed, hatred, and delusion—these all have remedies for every person."
First, regarding the five objects for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana-citta*),
concentration is named according to the specific power of its object;
for one who acts out of greed, the mind only becomes settled through the diligent practice and cultivation of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
The practitioner of equal proportions (samabhāgacarita) possesses all [five afflictions] in equal measure;
thus, they are able to practice whichever cultivation is appropriate for their conduct.
Therefore, it is said that for the practitioner of equal proportions, the mind abides within the five stages of settling the mind (pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana), yet their conduct is not yet pure.
Some say that this also eliminates afflictions, but that is incorrect.

The traditional explanation holds that the practice of counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*) removes both *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought). Now, however, it removes only *vitarka*.
Therefore, it is said that one investigates only the vitarka (applied thought),
not excluding the vicāra (sustained thought). Question:
Why are they not eliminated?
Because when one investigates with careful scrutiny of the object,
discursive thought (*vitarka*) then becomes distracted.

Having explained the elimination of vitarka, the text next provides a detailed analysis through questions and answers regarding the distinctions between those of "equal parts" (*samabhāga*) and those of "thin dust" (*tanubhūmi*).
First, it clarifies those of equal parts; subsequently, it clarifies those of thin dust.
Regarding the initial response concerning those of "equal proportions" (*samabhāga*) up to the phrase "neither superior nor excellent," Jing states:
"Those of equal proportions possess the propensities (*carita*) of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, discursive thought (*vitarka*), and so forth."
Unlike those whose practice is biased toward the intensification of greed and so forth,
this is not "superior" or "excellent";
nevertheless, such a person of balanced temperament may at times encounter conditions that lead them to cultivate the practice of impurity.
Alternatively, one may contemplate compassion and pity;
even when encountering conditions, contemplating *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) is similar in its mode of practice (*vipaśyanā*) to that of the partial [contemplation].
Master Ji says:
One who is a person of greedy temperament is called such because greed arises immediately upon encountering conditions;
persons of the other temperaments are likewise so named.
According to the conditions they encounter, greed and the rest arise immediately, and thus they are called "persons of greedy temperament" because they resemble greed and the others.
The following clarifies the practice of those with thin defilements.
First, seven phrases are listed;
next, they are explained, and finally, a conclusion is drawn.
In the commentary, the first section explains the absence of heavy obstructions.
This is because there are no three types of obstructions.
Regarding the statement, "As for the obstruction of karma, it can even obstruct the right path," and so forth:
That is to say: the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), other intentionally committed grave unwholesome karmas that invite rebirth in the three evil destinies;
furthermore, karma for an eighth existence, the female body, the northern continent (*uttarakuru*), and the non-conceptual heavens (*asaṃjñi-sattva*).
The arising of the fruit of that karma obstructs the Noble Path, preventing it from arising.
As for the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it consists of those [afflictions] that are of the highest degree, intense, long-lasting, and frequently recurring;
because of these, one is unable to achieve purification through the objects of pure conduct, such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), within this present life.
This is called the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the obstacle of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*), Jing says:
That is to say, if the place of birth reaches the point where the fruition of maturation arises,
yet because that very basis of maturation— which was summoned by a prior karmic obstruction— does not give rise to the Noble Path, it is therefore called an "obstruction of maturation."
If the Brahma King is a bodhisattva’s emanation, it is not an obstacle resulting from karmic maturation (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*);
if he were to actually experience [the state], it would be an obstacle of karmic maturation.
Alternatively, there may be places of birth where one becomes deaf, mute, or dull-witted.
Just as those in the three continents can receive human retribution, even those with illnesses such as deafness or idiocy should be able to give rise to the Noble Path;
yet, because of their deafness or idiocy, the Noble Path does not arise.
Ji says:
"Place of birth" refers to the specific location where one is born.
"The Noble Path does not depend upon that which is not born" refers to the three evil destinies.
Regarding "the fruition of maturation arising in such a place of birth," this means that the maturation of unwholesome karma arises in those places; it is not upon these that the Noble Path depends.
Second, regarding the initial attainment of purity:
this refers to those who possess well-purified ethical discipline (*śīla*) and upright view (*dṛṣṭi*).
Ethical discipline is the primary foundation for abandoning transgressions.
Right view is the foremost leader that gathers all virtues;
therefore, it is said that virtuous precepts are initially purified by right view.
Through these ten causes, the precepts are pure.
As previously stated in the twenty-eighth [section], there are ten factors conducive to training (*śaikṣa-dharma*).
The first is to avoid women and the like;
this is explained through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on upright view (*rju-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the phrase "generating even deep resolute conviction toward all Tathāgatas and noble disciples," this refers to the inconceivable supernormal powers,
pure lands, and places of birth of the Buddhas and noble disciples.
Regarding that profound teaching on suchness and the ineffable reality, they develop superior resolve without fear;
because they are free from deceit and guile, their view is upright, and they belong to the class of those who are upright.
Upright view that is free from guile and resembles true untainted right view is called "the category of right view.
Regarding the phrase "practicing correctly in accordance with the holy teachings":
whatever practice one cultivates and whatever level of realization one attains, whether shallow or deep, one personally realizes it exactly as it truly is, without exceeding its actual measure.
The three kinds of liberation have already been fully prepared.
Regarding the teaching of the Dharma and the teaching of its meaning:
the false teachings of non-Buddhists are called "non-Dharma."
Now, that which has attained the true teaching is called the "Teaching of the Dharma.
That which is spoken by non-Buddhists may contain some slight meaning or may be entirely devoid of meaning, and thus it is not called the "Teaching of Meaning.
That which is taught by the Buddha contains either much meaning or is entirely meaningful, and is therefore called the "Teaching of Meaning."
Those whose faculties are matured possess the five faculties beginning with faith and all seven material faculties in their entirety.
As for those who have accumulated the provisions for the present life:
This refers to having few desires, being content, and so forth.
Next, the explanation of the latter four phrases may be understood according to the text.
The fourteenth [section], the explanation of the synonyms for the *pudgala*,
has six parts.
The first is the explanation of the *śramaṇa*.
The text is divided into five sections:
first, the enumeration of names;
second, a brief assignment of categories.
Third, a brief explanation;
fourth, a detailed exposition;
fifth, citation of scriptural evidence.
