Regarding the "inconceivable nature of phenomena" (dharmatā), it is like the solidity of the earth and so forth.
Regarding the "abiding nature of phenomena," why is the world arranged in such a manner?
K’i says:
The wisdom subsumed by the three gates and six matters consists of four kinds of vipaśyanā;
each of these types of wisdom penetrates all three gates and six matters.
Regarding the statements "establishing the nature of phenomena," "the inconceivable nature of phenomena," and "the abiding nature of phenomena":
for example, establishing that sound is impermanent because it is produced establishes the nature of phenomena.
Like karma, medicinal herbs, and incantations,
this inconceivable nature of phenomena (dharmatā) refers to the seeds of natural law (dharmatā-bīja) and the distinctions between the lineages of the three vehicles.
This is called "abiding in the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*).

By investigating the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) within the second object and the third aspect, one gives rise to the cognition of the limits of things (*vastuparyantatā-jñāna*) and so forth.

By investigating the individual specific characteristics of form, sensation, and so on, and attaining the demarcation of phenomena (*dharmaparyanta*), one gives rise to the cognition of the limits of things and so forth.

By investigating the third characteristic—the common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa)—through the fourth category, the fifth time, and the sixth principle in accordance with the Dharma, one gives rise to realization as it truly is (yathābhūta-bodha).
Second, regarding the five perfections (pāramitās), one contemplates them individually by distinguishing six types of objects of focus (ālambana).
The text consists of five sections.
First, regarding the discernment of the contemplation of impurity,
one investigates six matters.
Regarding the statement therein that "foul odors arise from stench," Tai says: "For example,
when food has reached full maturity, it is called 'foul odor'."
That which has not yet reached the stage of full ripening is called "putrid.
Ji (基) says:
because it undergoes transformation and decay, it is foul-smelling and thus termed "malodorous."
For example, things such as excrement and filth are called "stinking upon arising" because they become foul as soon as they are produced;
examples include garlic and leeks.
In the investigation of external specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), nine types of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) are distinguished.
It should be understood that the following three transformations correspond to these nine aspects:
namely, starting from "blood," "protection," and so forth.
Jingyun said:
"The belly serves as a cauldron of blood because it contains much hot blood.
Tai said: [as above].
If one dies naturally, the blood flows internally until it is exhausted;
if killed by another, the blood flows externally until it is exhausted.
Thus, the six types of blood flow until they are completely spent.
This is what that refers to. Ji said:
"The head, body, and belly here constitute the cauldron of blood."
Because it can contain and ripen blood.
Regarding the first [type], which is a mere conventional designation for the appearance of a skeleton made of wood, stone, clay, or the like, painted with colors—
the Tripiṭaka Master says:
When wishing to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*),
one first contemplates a skeleton.
Tai [Shi] said:
When a practitioner of meditation wishes to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) but cannot find any actual bones,
they fashion a skeleton out of wood, stone, or other materials to practice the contemplation of impurity.
Since these are not actual bones, it is merely called a "skeleton" (*kaṅkāla*).
If one attains the contemplation of actual bones as impure, it is only then called the "contemplation of the skeleton.
By this principle, the ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*) are distinguished:
whether it be "bones," "skeleton," or "bones and skeleton," these are all categories of transformation and decay.
In this way, the bones, skeletons, and so forth, after the passage of days and months,
undergo destruction through their own nature;
or they are destroyed by others, such as being burned by fire or rotted by water.
Regarding the investigation of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*):
at that time, the practitioner knows that while the pure form (*rūpa*) of his own internal body has not yet decayed,
it is nevertheless similar to the external body in its state of having already undergone transformation and decay, for their nature of transformation and decay is identical.
This is called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
As for the time of investigation:
it refers to when both internal pure forms and external impure forms are present simultaneously.
In this present life, those pure physical forms that previously existed and have now ceased, though one has already died, continue to arise as various impure manifestations;
yet, at present, I still possess what appears to be a pure physical form.
In future ages, it is impossible that there should not be impurity, just as there is impurity in external forms in the present.
Within the investigation of principles,
to say "it is thus named" refers to investigating those principles by means of the conventional, the ultimate, and the principle of dependence upon causes and conditions.
Jingyun: It was previously stated that there is no self, and that purity and impurity are spoken of merely as conventional designations.
This is called the principle of ultimate relativity.

Next, it is explained that life-force (*jīvitendriya*), heat (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—which are preceded by past karma and afflictions (*kleśa*)—temporarily appear as pure and so forth;
this is called the principle of dependence on causes and conditions (*hetupratyayāpekṣā-yukti*) according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
Jì (基) says:
The previous explanation that the absence of a self within is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) was so stated;
furthermore, as it is said, everything from the visualization of a livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) up to the chain of bones (*asthi-śaṅkalā*) is conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
This present conclusion follows the sequence of the discourse rather than being arranged according to a systematic order.
Furthermore, the sequence for binding [the mudrās] and the corresponding meditations can be understood accordingly.
Now, to explain:
the absence of self both internally and externally, conventionally designated as "pure" and "impure," is the ultimate principle of relative dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
Furthermore, as it is said: "Even up to the skeleton is called the conventional principle of dependence (*saṃvṛti-apekṣā-yukti*).
Regarding the statement, "This present body of mine is produced by the karma and afflictions of previous lives," and so forth:
This is called the principle of causal dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
As it says below: "I myself am able to directly perceive within and without the body" refers to the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of visual consciousness;
up to "being able to sever craving" refers to the direct perception of the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).

That is to say, one reflects thus: "How can the mental application that contemplates the remedial factors now serve as an antidote to the afflictions that are about to arise within the objective sphere of those very remedies?"
Master Ji explains the meaning herein as follows:
External objects of impurity are called "antidotes" because they counteract sensual desire;
by taking such impure forms as an object, one will necessarily be able to counteract the afflictions that would otherwise arise toward pure objects.
That is to say, one formulates the syllogism as follows:
"When taking impurity as an object, one ought to be able to produce desire and greed,
because it takes that which is capable of acting as an antidote as its object."
Just as when one takes the signless (*animitta*) as an object, one can dispel the sign (*nimitta*),
the second [section] clarifies the cultivation of the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*):
it consists of investigating the six matters through the contemplation of their distinct objects.
This may be understood from the text.
Regarding the third section of the thirty-first fascicle, which clarifies the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
it consists of the thorough investigation of the six factors for the arising of all phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "the arising of this and that dharma," it means that because each preceding member arises, each subsequent member arises;
and because each preceding member ceases, each subsequent member ceases.
Within this, there is absolutely no autonomous creator, nor indeed any transformer of phenomena.
This refutes the non-Buddhist calculation that Īśvara is the creator, the producer, and the destroyer.

Furthermore, it refutes the Sāṃkhya calculation that there exists a primal nature (prakṛti) termed "self-nature" (svabhāva), and their calculation of a self-principle termed "the person" (puruṣa); the remaining twenty-three principles are termed "intermediate," because they are that which is transformed.
Regarding "whether internal or external":
among the twelve links [of dependent origination], those subsumed under the sense faculties (indriya) are called internal;
those subsumed under the objects (viṣaya) are called external.
Regarding the phrases "ignorance of the prior limit" and "ignorance of the posterior limit," etc.:
the ten causes of the past draw forth the birth-and-death of the present;
for the time being, ignorance is cited as an example.
Therefore, it is said that there is ignorance regarding the past limit.
Regarding the present, ten causes draw forth future birth and death;
for now, only ignorance is cited.
Therefore, it is said that ignorance pertains to the future limit (*aparānta*).
Such a conceptual differentiation of the nature of the twelve links is called their "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
This is when one investigates the principle [of dependent origination].
One performs the initial investigation by means of the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*),

which is as follows: one observes that it is only in dependence upon karma and its fruit that ignorance and so forth are conventionally designated as "agent" and "experiencer," yet there is absolutely no real agent or experiencer.
Furthermore, within this there are two kinds of fruits and two kinds of causes.
Regarding the two kinds of fruits:
the first is the fruit of self-nature (*svabhāva-phala*).
Regarding the dharmas such as the six sense bases that arise from maturation in this present life:
the six faculties and the six objects are called the fruit of self-substance,
while the two types of feeling are called the fruit of the enjoyment of objects.
Regarding the phrase "arising through the predominance of karma that is either pleasant or unpleasant," this refers to the six types of sensation experiencing the six sense objects.
The objects are what is experienced, and sensation is that which experiences.
Regarding the two causes:
first, the projecting cause; second, the producing cause.
The projecting cause refers to the seeds of the two realms, up to and including contact and sensation.
Due to being deluded regarding the two kinds of results previously explained, ignorance arises;
from ignorance, volitional formations (saṃskāra) are produced;
and these formations are capable of inducing the seeds for the designation "consciousness" (vijñāna).
The seeds of names-and-words further give rise to the seeds of name-and-form;
the seeds of name-and-form further induce the seeds of the six sense bases;
and the seeds of the six sense bases further induce the seeds of contact.
Furthermore, the seed of contact draws forth the seed of feeling;
in this way, these seven factors sequentially induce one another.
As the Tripiṭaka Master says:
The projecting cause (ākṣepa-hetu) specifically grasps the essence of wholesome and unwholesome karma; however,
in this present text, it generally refers to the ignorance that serves as the cause of formations (saṃskāra) and the seeds of the five members projected by those formations,
collectively naming them the projecting cause.
The following explains the intended meaning of "mutual attraction":
it is for the sake of causing the sequential arising of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—comprised within the members of future existence.
Thus, first appropriating the seeds of those dharmas is what is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*).
In this way, these seven branches, in relation to birth, old age, and death, give rise to consciousness and the other factors;
all of them constitute the nature of the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
As for what is called "consciousness subsumed under ideation" (*saṃjñā-saṃgṛhīta-vijñāna*):
"Perception" refers to consciousness as it is subsumed under the branch of "arising.
As for the cause of arising, it means when one experiences the feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance, and so forth.
While currently experiencing the feelings associated with the objective sphere that are subsumed under old age and death from the past,
one also gives rise to craving for a future existence.
With these two types of craving as conditions, grasping arises.
Therefore, it is said that they are able to encompass all forms of grasping belonging to the category of craving and the category of delusion.
Grasping is the intensification of craving; because it is an intensification of craving, it is called "grasping.
Thus, the four types of grasping have craving as their essence.
Therefore, it is said that all forms of grasping (*upādāna*) belong to the category of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Furthermore, this grasping is associated with ignorance (*moha*), and thus it is also said to belong to the category of ignorance.

By means of this craving and grasping acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), they moisten the seeds of the eight members [of dependent origination], causing the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth—which have been projected—to produce their matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
He then stated that the three links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are called the causes for arising.
The Tripitaka Master said:
"The causes for arising are explicitly taken up within the textual passage concerning craving and grasping."
The craving produced by feeling is designated as the cause of arising.
Because of the dominant power of these two causes, one is pursued by the three types of suffering and draws together this entire mass of pure great suffering.
Regarding the two causes, the preceding ten members are explained as the essence of these two causes.
Once the causes are established, the three types of suffering follow upon the attainment of the fruit.
Fourth, the explanation of the contemplation of the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*) is as follows:
Investigating the six matters: regarding the investigation of how,
by taking the six elements of the past, future, and present as conditions, one enters the mother’s womb and so forth— this means that,

having relinquished the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one enters the mother’s womb by depending upon the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*), space, and consciousness, and by relying upon the impure [factors].
Furthermore, by means of the causes and conditions consisting of the various karmas and afflictions of past lives, as well as the seeds of one's own designations and names,
one fully understands the meaning of "contingent dependence" (*apekṣā*).
Regarding what is called "establishing the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*) within the principle of "reasoning according to the nature of things" (*dharmatā-yukti*):
Just as the natures of the four great elements— solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion— are established by their own nature and do not depend on causes and conditions,
so too is the inconceivable dharma-nature.
One should not contemplate why the earth is solid rather than moist and so forth.
For those who abide in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
the earth is eternally solid whether a Buddha appears or does not appear.

Fifth, it clarifies the investigation of ānāpānasmṛti by means of six matters: that is, relying on the Buddha’s teaching, one is able to correctly understand the objects of inhalation and exhalation, binding the mind to them with thorough comprehension and without forgetfulness.
This is the meaning of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
Furthermore, one contemplates that those breaths are "internal" because they can be apprehended within the body and are thus connected to the body;
they are "external" because they belong to the category of external wind and are therefore subsumed under the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
The distinction between internal and external is called "knowledge of the object.
Furthermore, one should contemplate that both inhalation and exhalation each have two aspects:
first, inhalation; second, intermediate inhalation.
The same applies to the exhalation.
Furthermore, one knows that such inhalations and exhalations are long when their arising and continuity persist for a long duration;
likewise, one knows that such inhalations and exhalations are short.
The brief arising of intermediate inhalation and exhalation is termed "short.
Having thus contemplated the distinctions of the six matters based on the object of purification (śubha-viṣaya),
he concludes and points them out.
The preceding five types of concentration through mental observation are termed "objects of focus for purifying conduct" (*caritaviśodhana*).

This continues until the passage: "As for the objects of focus for skillfulness (*kauśalyālambana*) and the objects of focus for purifying afflictions (*kleśaviśodhana*), I shall explain them in their respective places later. Below this...
The discernment of skillful objects and the objects for purifying afflictions are termed "one's own domain.
The preceding extensive passages collectively constitute the second section, clarifying that one-pointedness of mind applies to both śamatha and vipaśyanā.
From here below is the third section, which clarifies the nine kinds of preparatory practices (*prayoga*).

Within this, first there is a general enumeration of nine items each for both the black and white categories; subsequently, the nine names of the white category are listed individually and distinguished by contrast with their counterparts.
Next, the nine types of the white category (śukla-pakṣa) are explained individually;
finally, these two categories are summarized to distinguish their direct and inverse sequences,
collectively termed the eighteen obstacles and remedies, which constitute one-pointedness of mind (citta-ekāgratā).
Regarding the statement that "by means of these nine types of preparatory practices (prayoga) subsumed under the white category (śuklapakṣa), one’s mind can swiftly attain concentration":
this refers to the ability to swiftly attain concentration by performing these nine preparatory practices within the states of mind resulting from hearing and reflection (śruta-mayī and cintā-mayī).
Regarding "causing samādhi to progress further":
this refers to the fact that by performing the nine preparatory applications (*prayoga*) with a concentrated mind, one is able to cause meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) to progress further.
Furthermore, because of this, one is able to proceed swiftly and without delay toward the stage to be reached and whatever is to be attained therein.
One who wishes to give rise to supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to travel to other realms, as well as to cultivate and produce qualities according to one's desire,
achieves these aims swiftly through these nine types of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Regarding the specific explanations that follow, one should understand that the preparatory application is to be added to each [case] individually.
This means that for one who is dominated by desire, the medicine of the contemplation of impurity and so forth corresponds to the ailment.

Second, regarding those who have practiced application: they have previously cultivated the categories of calm abiding and insight extensively, or at least to some degree, such that they are not beginners in all meditative practices.
Why is this? The passage beginning with "Because...
cites the initial stage of practice to demonstrate that one has already become habituated to it through repeated training;
this constitutes the third [type of] non-lax application of effort (*apramāda-prayoga*).
This refers to initiating uninterrupted and earnest practice.
Second, regarding the cultivation of harmonious respect,
this refers to the six points of harmony and respect.
Fourth is unerring application:
just as the teacher has brought about awakening,
one trains accordingly, free from self-conceit and the like.
Fifth is timely application (*kālaprayoga*):
practicing tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) according to their respective times;
furthermore, being able to discern the essential characteristics and the appropriate timing for the four factors of tranquility, insight (*vipaśyanā*), exertion, and equanimity.
The essence of *śamatha* is precisely the nine stages of mental abiding (*navākārā cittasthiti*).
There are two aspects of *śamatha*:

first, the aspect of the object of focus (*ālambananimitta*), which is the image (*pratibimba*) that is a counterpart (*sabhāga*) to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) known by the category of *śamatha*; this is the object of focus for *śamatha*.
Regarding the second causal characteristic, the original intent is as follows: one practices *śamatha* by means of its cultivation through habitual perfuming;

however, fearing that the mind may sink due to this reliance on *śamatha*, one practices the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of *vipaśyanā* in order to cause the settled mind to depart from sinking and attain purity.
The preparatory application of cultivation, when compared to pure *śamatha*, constitutes its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
What is meant by "insight" (*vipaśyanā*)? It refers to the practice of insight by way of the four modes of conduct, the three gateways, and the six distinct objects of observation.
Immediately following in the previous fascicle, it says: "There are four kinds of vipaśyanā;
namely, that which is able to correctly discern, most thoroughly discern, universally investigate, and universally examine—these are called the four modes of activity."
As for the three gates:
first, practice that follows only the characteristics;
second, practice that follows discursive investigation.
Third is the practice of investigative examination (*anupaśyanā*).
These six matters are: meaning, thing, characteristic, category, time, and principle.
Regarding the observation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are two types.
First, the characteristic of the object of focus refers to the image of the objective essence of the category of what is known through observation, which arises in accordance with the observing mind.
Second, the characteristic of the causal condition refers to the mind that has been perfumed by vipaśyanā.

Fearing that the mind of observation may become too buoyant and agitated, one practices the preparatory applications of *śamatha* in order to cause the observing mind to be free from agitation and attain purity; these serve as the causal conditions for the subsequent *vipaśyanā*.
"Or fearing the time of sinking" refers to knowing when the mind is weak and inferior, and fearing it will sink into dullness.
Regarding "being pliant, upright, and so forth in the categories of śamatha and vipaśyanā":
the equilibrium of śamatha and vipaśyanā is termed "pliant and upright."
Regarding the phrase "the characteristic of equanimity refers to that which causes the mind to become equanimous toward its object," Jing says:
"It is the ultimate abandonment of laxity and excitement that causes the mind to become equanimous."
If one's diligence is excessive, the mind becomes restless;
therefore, one must not be overly diligent.
Tai said:
When one is utterly free from both subsiding and excitation regarding the object of focus,
this is called the time of equanimity as a predominant condition; that is to say, when one has just become free from agitation within the categories of calm abiding and insight,
this is the time for cultivating equanimity.

One should also say that when the mind has already been liberated from all sinking within the categories of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), this is the time for cultivating equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Sixth is the application of thorough comprehension (*parijñā-prayoga*):

it means that regarding the various signs thus described, one skillfully grasps and thoroughly understands them, such that one is able to enter, abide in, and emerge from all meditative concentrations at will.

At times, when one abandons the mental image of the meditative object and attends with mental attention to the actual entities that serve as objects for the distracted mind of the desire realm, this is called the "application of thorough comprehension."
This refers to how the image (pratibimba) within the objective part (nimittabhāga) of the concentrated mind, when clearly understood,
resembles the nature of the object perceived by the distracted mind;
this is what is called "discarding the image to contemplate the substance."
The Tripitaka Master says:
One abandons the mental image that was the object of focus within meditative concentration and instead takes as the object the actual substance of the skeleton within the original grove.
The seventh and eighth [stages] may be understood accordingly.
The ninth stage, the section on the practice of correct application, is divided into two parts.
First, a brief indication of its characteristics.
Second, regarding the correct elimination [of obstacles], there is a detailed explanation in five sections.
In the first section, concerning "the objects of focus" up to "all signs of impurity," one first contemplates the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*).
Next, one abandons the contemplation of the bloated corpse;
next, one again abandons the contemplation of the putrefying and other such signs.
One then gives rise to mental attention by means of removing these objective signs.
The repeated and correct elimination of the focal object so that distinct objects appear before one is called "correct application" (*samyak-prayoga*).
This is according to the detailed explanation.
First is the enumeration, followed by the explanation,
and finally the selection and clarification.
In the explanation, "not taking up" means not grasping at any characteristics and not engaging in mental recollection.
Regarding the phrase "because one contemplates the objects of another meditative stage by means of that other meditative stage, it is called 'attention directed toward another'":
this refers to cases such as the first dhyāna taking phenomena of a higher stage as its object, or a dhyāna of a higher stage taking phenomena of a lower stage as its object, and so forth.
The name "conditioned by objects of other meditative stages" is analyzed into two parts to clarify what is being explained. First,
there is a general heading that identifies the two types of objects to be clarified.
Second, the presentation of its characteristics.
Within the preceding section,
although there are generally five types of characteristics for correctly eliminating all objects of focus once they have been fully established, [the following applies].
However, within this context, the intended meaning is that one internally withdraws the mind and does not attend to mental engagement (*manasikāra*).
Herein, the ninth [stage] clarifies the correct application (*prayoga*),
for it is precisely capable of dispelling the signs of the focal object (*ālambana-nimitta*).
Within these, the first involves inwardly withdrawing the mind;
the second consists of the mental application of non-attention toward all signs;
the third still takes the objects of other stages as its focal point.
The fourth still contemplates objects such as the impure;
the fifth still takes the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*) as its object and applies mental attention to it.
Therefore, these latter three do not accord with the practice of eliminating [obstacles] during formal application (*prayoga*).
Second, within the section on the characteristics of the correct application (*samyak-prayoga*), he explains the characteristic of the mental attention of non-recollection (*amanasikāra*).
Second, from "furthermore, practicing with signs and with conceptualization" onwards, he explains the internal withdrawal of the mind.
Regarding the "prior" [stage]:
this refers to a beginner who, at all times, does not bind the mind to the objects of the five stabilizing practices;

they merely maintain mindfulness so as to avoid distraction, and eventually, having ceased all mental activity, they experience internal well-being and lack discursive thought regarding external signs.
Having eliminated the focal object,
one experiences a sense of pliancy while practicing cultivation;
this is the second [stage], which internally gathers the mind within.

The structure consists of the initial statement of the principle (*dharma*), followed by the illustration (*udāharaṇa*), and finally the application (*anusandhi*). Regarding the first part, which states:

"Furthermore, one proceeds toward objects such as those with signs, conceptual differentiation, and impurity," this clarifies that by means of non-mental engagement (*amanasikāra*), one grasps external signs and objects such as impurity.
"How does one practice... down to neither grasping nor abandoning?
Below, this explains the meaning of "neither abandoning nor grasping.

Because the practice proceeds by way of settling upon the object of focus (*ālambana*), it is not called "abandoning," and so forth, up to being unable to proceed toward or realize the objects and phenomena that are to be known.
This is the reverse explanation.
From the phrase "by means of counting, conviction, and successive removal," it follows as a direct explanation.
"For example, as in the world" below;
this is the second instance where an analogy is raised to clarify it.
"The principle herein" below.
The third combined analogy:

regarding the statement "having generated resolve (*adhimukti*) toward a narrow and limited object, one then correctly eliminates that very narrow and limited [object]," it should be understood that this is just as when, having first generated resolve by observing a narrow and limited blue, one then eliminates the observation of a vast blue or an immeasurable blue; the subsequent elimination should be known to be likewise.
Having already eliminated a limited amount of blue, one may again form a resolute conviction regarding a limited amount of yellow,
or one may form a resolute conviction regarding vast blue or immeasurable blue.
Regarding the statement "one should know that it is likewise for the vast and the immeasurable":
having taken as an object a vast blue, one subsequently eliminates it and contemplates a vast yellow;
or, whether it be immeasurable blue or limited blue, the same applies to all immeasurable [colors].
If the various characteristics, images, and manifestations of material phenomena appear, one should know that they are coarse and similar to transformations (*nirmāṇa*).
If the images of material phenomena are taken as objects, they are coarse.
It is like a transformation.
Regarding the manifestation of images through the dominant power of what was previously experienced, which is designated by the provisional name "all formless phenomena":
this is because when one contemplates the formless, other apprehended phenomena lack any objective characteristics.
Due to the predominant power of seeking and apprehending names,
an image appears.
What is the essential nature of such an image?
The Tripitaka Master says:
The images produced by non-material dharmas, such as feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā), according to conditions,
are themselves the essential nature and category of the original substance.
This is called "those dharmas.
Next is the explanation of purifying hindrances;
herein there are two parts.
First, the purification of obstacles is explained;
second, the practice that can purify obstacles is analyzed by means of four propositions.
Within the first [section], there is first a general presentation and enumeration.
Next, the detailed explanation follows.
Within this, there are two sections;
in the first section:
The hindrance of cowardice refers to the longing for,
lack of joy in, and anxious distress regarding defiled phenomena when one is diligently practicing the dharma of renunciation that leads to nirvāṇa,
as well as the dharmas of detachment pertaining to the mundane and supramundane paths.
Therefore, the mind becomes timid and weak.
As for the "discursive thoughts that act as obstacles," these refer to discursive thoughts such as desire, ill-will, and harmfulness.

Furthermore, one withdraws the mind into internal tranquility.
In this context, the sense organs of oneself and others are termed "internal," while the objects that support those organs are termed "external."
Furthermore, one may take the impurity within the bodies of oneself or others and designate it as "internal";
if one takes the external appearance of the bodies of oneself or others as impure, it is designated as "external.
Regarding the category of śamatha, this extends even to those who cultivate the contemplation of feelings, mind, and phenomena internally.
By means of the mind of hearing, one grasps those six perceptions and internally condenses them together with the four aggregates that accompany them;
this is called the cultivation of the contemplation of internal feelings, mind, and phenomena.
To collect the mind and abide within the six perceptions is termed "internal condensation."
Because the nature and characteristics of the four aggregates, such as feeling and so forth—which are non-material—are unmixed, they are called "undisturbed.
Alternatively, because they are the objects of meditative concentration, they are also called "undisturbed.
Regarding the category of non-distraction:
This refers to the four formless aggregates that were previously grasped by you with a distracted mind as objects of perception, which have now passed away and ceased;

and it also refers to the four formless aggregates that are currently being grasped as signs, through discursive thought and secondary afflictions, due to a lapse in mindfulness during the present practice of contemplation.
You should, with a mind of hearing and reflection, investigate this according to reason:
that the nature of these four aggregates is deceptive and illusory, appearing abruptly and fraught with many faults, and thus cannot be relied upon.
This is called the cultivation of the contemplation of feelings, mind, and phenomena with respect to the external.
Tai says:
"The function of the mental abiding (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding the internal is superior to that of the external."
Not being conditioned by the five desires is called non-distraction.
Regarding the category of vipaśyanā, from the observation of feelings, mind, and dharmas internally and externally, the four aggregates observed within—
namely internal feeling, mind, and dharmas— are what is meant by a non-distracted mind.
Grasping at signs and discriminating extremes are called external feelings, mind, and dharmas.
Furthermore, you should, following the application of the foundations of mindfulness, proceed to the second instruction:
relying on a village to guard body and mind.
Regarding the statement, "If one should not exert the faculties and so forth toward such objective signs," Jing says:
"If one should not exert the faculties toward defiled objects, one must not apply effort."
If you encounter conditions favorable to the arising of wholesome states, you should exert effort to restrain the faculties and sever the path of speech.
Tai said:

When entering a village, if one encounters unwholesome objects and fails to restrain the sense faculties, or if one sees women, one must immediately restrain the sense faculties and abide in right mindfulness.
As it is said: "One whose conduct is dominated by desire is disciplined by the contemplation of impurity," and so forth.
Regarding the second category, the remaining four meditative stabilizations are first presented collectively as being similar in type,
and subsequently their specific differences are revealed.
The contemplation of impurity.
This is divided into four parts;
first, the explanation of the contemplation of loving-kindness.
This is further divided into two parts:
first, the cultivation of the perception of joy toward sentient beings of the three categories;
second, the section beginning with "Furthermore, not abandoning them... and so forth.
Regarding "clearly entering the applications of mindfulness through compassionate conduct":
as for the phrase "faultless sensual pleasures and so forth" mentioned previously,
this refers to faultless sensual pleasures within the desire realm.
In the first and second dhyāna stages, there is faultless joy and bliss;
in the third dhyāna stage, there is faultless bliss free from joy.
This is stated in the second passage.
It is said that others also [apply this] to those [beings], up to: "This is called one who practices the contemplation of the body in the external body.
As for all other sentient beings, they are likewise described as being among one's own kin, enemies, or neutral parties, and among the kin, enemies, or neutral parties of those families.
Just as I desire to turn away from suffering, those dear ones and enemies likewise desire to turn away from suffering.
When one reflects in this way, it is called practicing the contemplation of the body in relation to external bodies.
"If it is so for me, it is likewise for all those sentient beings.
Just as my own self has those who are friends, enemies,
and neutral persons, so too do all those sentient beings.
There are those who are friends, enemies, and neutral parties.
Just as I myself desire to attain supreme happiness, so it is with all those sentient beings.
Thus, although there are friends, enemies, and neutral parties for me...
Yet, while seeking their own superior happiness,
those sentient beings— whether they be friends, enemies, or neutral persons—
likewise seek to attain superior happiness for themselves.
"Those sentient beings who are equal to oneself" clarifies the bestowing of happiness upon one's own body and the bodies of others as being equal.
In the text, it simply states that because they are equal to oneself and similar to oneself, one should bestow happiness upon them.
Knowing that one should likewise bestow happiness upon others as one does upon oneself,
and giving to both self and others alike,
is called the cultivation of the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal and external.
Tài said:
"Just as I desire to turn my back on suffering,
so too do all those sentient beings desire to turn their backs on suffering."
"I shall provide them with benefit and happiness"—
this is called internal and external observation.

These four foundations of mindfulness, when explained collectively in terms of the aggregates, are termed the "foundations of mindfulness of the analysis of objects" (*vibhanga-smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth.
This explains that the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) which takes the five aggregates as its general object is called "the mindfulness of phenomena with mixed objects.
As for the specific cultivation of the mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna), it takes only visible colors such as blue, shapes such as long, and the bodily intimation of bodily action.
Because one generates resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the three categories,
the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established. T'ai says:

If the four foundations of mindfulness have already reached maturity and one takes all the aggregates as a collective object, it is called the foundation of mindfulness with respect to the disintegration of objects;
if, at the time of the preparatory application, one grasps only the characteristic of form, it is exclusively the foundation of mindfulness of the body.

Regarding the passage, "Furthermore, by relying on the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), one can correctly enter into the mental application of reality (*tattva-manasikāra*)":

thus far, it has been explained in general that one provisionally establishes three categories—friends, enemies, and neutral parties—among all sentient beings through the exercise of resolute conviction.
Now, it clarifies the entry into reality.
The superior resolve (*adhimukti*) is as stated in the text. Tai says:
Because all that exists in the prior limit consists of three categories of reality that transcend the three categories of conceptual construction and the finite,
there is not even the slightest portion of [the categories of] friend, enemy, or neutral party.
This is as explained in the section on comparative analysis below.
Tài said:
"If true compassion-vision were divided into one hundred parts,
even the most complete form of conceptualized compassion and conceptualized pity would not equal even one part of those one hundred."
Furthermore, if one were to divide actual observation into a thousand parts, conceptual visualization would not equal even one-thousandth of it;
continuing in this manner, even if conceptual visualization were divided into as many parts as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, actual observation would still surpass each of them.
If further subdivided, it would not even equal one *aupamika* fraction;
as for the *aupaniṣadika* fraction, it is the greatest and most ultimate among numbers, having no name by which it can be translated.
"Other matters are as previously explained" means that some interpret "other matters" as being like the aforementioned contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Now, this concludes the explanation of the section on the gates of manifesting distinctions.
The other methods may be understood by analogy with what is explained in the section on the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Second, regarding the explanation of the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
first is the observation of dependent origination itself.
Second, proceeding from dependent origination toward the foundations of mindfulness:
for a beginner practitioner up until the point of experiencing the future aggregate of pure great suffering,
it means that the beginner practitioner understands through the general conceptualization of hearing and reflection.
It means that because sentient beings are deluded, they perceive what is impermanent, impure, suffering, and non-self as being permanent, pleasurable, self, and pure; thus, there are four inversions.
Through these inversions born of delusion, they give rise to various karmas, which serve as their cause.
One gives rise to craving for what is presently being experienced,
and one gives rise to craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*) regarding the various self-bodies that will arise hereafter.
Through these two types of craving, they moisten the fundamental karma previously created for birth, thereby bringing about the acquisition of a future mass of pure and great suffering.
This is the observation of others.
From here on, observing oneself is likewise generated.

If one attends to and contemplates the nature of conditions and dependent origination regarding the aggregates of oneself and others, as they come and go, this is called dwelling in the contemplation of internal and external body, feeling, mind, and phenomena.
If one takes as an object the aggregates already experienced by oneself or others in the past, they are called "internal";
the aggregates not yet experienced in the future are called "external.
This is explained in the third [section], the contemplation of the six elements.
First, one contemplates the internal and external elements in general;
second, under the heading "furthermore, there is another method," one contemplates only the six elements within the internal body.
Within the former [first method], there are again three parts.
First, one contemplates the six coarse elements.
Second, within these four great elements, one further applies mental visualization to break down the coarse by means of the subtle.
Third, regarding one's own body, one clarifies the entry into the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

To understand that within this body composed of the four great elements there exists the realm, lineage, and individual nature of all seeds of consciousness is to rely on the principle of "conforming and evolving.
Within the body of the four great elements and five sense faculties, there exist the seeds of all consciousnesses.
To speak fully, one should say that within the four great elements, the five sense faculties, and the six consciousnesses, all seeds of form and mind are present.
Now, this is stated briefly: within the body composed of the four great elements, there exist all the seed-elements of the various consciousnesses.
The coarse is analyzed by means of the subtle.
This section consists of four parts;
first, the analysis of the four great elements.
Second, analyze the element of space.
Third, analyze the element of consciousness.
Fourth, analyze the ten material elements.
It is like breaking down the four great elements.
Tai says:
"Because it is for the sake of the conditions that sustain the body, one swallows; this is what is meant by 'swallowing'."
The place where one swallows is called "swallowing.
Regarding the second [section], which observes only the six elements within one's own body,
the text is divided into two parts.
First, one practices the contemplation of resolute conviction;
second, one practices the contemplation of reality.
Within the former, there are again two [subdivisions].
First, the contemplation of water, fire, earth, wind, and space is explained;
subsequently, it is summarized that one enters the differentiation of the elements through the preparatory practice of impurity and cultivates the meditation on the body.
Within this, regarding the contemplation of reality:

The phrase "it is said that by means of such an attention of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa-manasikāra), up to the characteristic of the realm of space" refers back to the aforementioned attention of resolute conviction:
"The various realms through which I have passed in the beginningless flow of saṃsāra are immeasurable and boundless, far exceeding this."
The various realms traversed throughout beginningless birth and death far exceed these six elements—earth and so forth—as observed through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Below, fire, water, earth, wind, space, and consciousness are explained.
Observe them in their respective order.
Regarding the fourth section, the text on the explanation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), there are three parts.
First is the correct observation of the wind of the breath.
Second, explaining the entry into the application of mindfulness of the body;
third, exhorting the cultivation of the preparatory practice (*prayoga*).
Within the first [section], the initial part explains the skillful means (*upāya*).
Because one has previously well-grasped the characteristics of houses, windows, doors, and so forth;
Tai [Hui] says:
"One forms a mental image of them as being gathered externally."
Like a bag filled with wind moving back and forth;
contemplate within that it is like the wind of the breath moving back and forth.
One correctly attends only to these two internal entrances and exits of the wind of the breath.
Within this, first take up the subtle breath-wind as it moves back and forth through the coarse apertures at the region of the heart and chest;
next, gradually take up many winds,
until finally all winds throughout every pore are followed into entry.
In this way, all the wind-aggregates that follow the various parts of the body,
as well as immeasurable wind-aggregates, are accumulated therein.
This is the second clarification regarding the entry into the three contemplations within the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The third [point] says: "Furthermore, if one generates resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) at the time when one is about to die oneself, and so forth,
by virtue of the nature of things (*dharmatā*), it is called 'abiding in the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal and external body.'"
If one takes as an object one's own body at the point of death when the breath has not yet ceased,
or if one takes as an object the breath-wind that has already ceased at the point of death, this is called "taking the internal as an object.
Such a principle exists by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*).
While the breath has not yet ceased,
the cessation is termed "conditioned by the internal.
Once the breath has ceased, the cessation is termed "conditioned by the external."
Taken together, these two types are called "cultivating the contemplation of the body by dwelling on the internal and external.
Regarding the exhortation to practice the preparatory application, it says: "Throughout all correct preparatory applications, one should understand it as previously explained."
Jingyun said:
"I exhort those who are beginners to cultivate, throughout all nine types of correct preparatory applications,
such unerring applications as are subsumed within this chapter on the cessation of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna)."
Regarding the remaining eight types within the stage of correct application (*samyak-prayoga*), as previously explained,
I shall now briefly clarify the meaning of the various categories of the meditation on breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*).
Among the nine applications, there is the application that accords with the non-perverted (*anuloma-aviparyāsa-prayoga*).
The remaining categories of meaning should be understood according to the characteristics of the previously explained meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, one may summarize that the four meditations beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*) differ from the meditation on impurity in their categories of meaning; they are subsumed under the category of tranquility (*śamatha*) and constitute unerring preparatory application (*prayoga*).
All other aspects of meaning should be understood by analogy with what was previously explained regarding the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Thus far, the five types of contemplation have been taught for beginners.
Hereafter, secondly, it is clarified how a beginner, practicing according to the instructions, attains the meditative absorption of the form realm (*rūpa-dhyāna*).
The text is divided into four parts.
First, it clarifies that at the time of correct practice, three benefits are accomplished.
The first is "ardor."
Second, possessing correct knowledge and mindfulness;
third, subduing greed and anxiety.
Within this, the enumeration, explanation, and conclusion follow the text.
The second section, "When one first initiates such correct application," explains how the preceding stage induces the subsequent one.
The third section, "In this way, up until those aforementioned signs appear," explains the gradual increase of practice.
Regarding the statement that "when the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are dispelled, contemplation with signs (*sanimitta-bhāvanā*) gradually becomes relaxed":
it is called "relaxed" because, as pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) first arises, [the afflictions] are gradually abandoned and extinguished.
T’ai says:
Prior to attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one experiences a sensation as if a heavy object were rising upon the crown of one's head;
subsequently, the entire body becomes pliant and tranquil.
From this point onward, the beginner is designated as being "with applied attention" (*samanaskāra*).
This explains the attainment of the dhyāna of the form realm.
Within this, it first explains the mental attention (*manasikāra*) for attaining concentration,
and subsequently explains the characteristics of one who possesses such mental attention.
